The kettle that knows when you are coming home
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 147 words

A washing machine which develops a fault can now report it before you notice. A central heating system that can access the GPS in your phone knows how far away you are and starts warming the house accordingly. This is the Internet of Things: ordinary objects, which have never needed to communicate before, quietly connected to a network.

Songdo, a city in South Korea where every home has ultra high-speed broadband, was built to demonstrate what happens when all of it works together. Waste is collected through underground pipes. Nobody, as far as anybody can tell, has ever seen a bin lorry.

The devices that get most attention are the silly ones — the fridge that orders milk — but the useful examples are duller. An internet-connected insulin pump, which sends readings straight to a doctor, is the sort of thing that will matter.

steps.answer: Ordinary objects, which never needed to communicate before, connected to a network.

steps.title: Every connected device can be hacked
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 149 words

The engineers who design these systems do not disagree with the people who worry about them. They simply put the risk differently. Anything that can send data can be made to send it somewhere else.

A smoke detector which reports to a phone is also a smoke detector which can be told to say nothing. A car whose in-built computer goes online when it develops a fault is a car that somebody else can go online to. Neither of these is a reason to stop, but both are reasons to ask who is responsible.

The second worry, which is raised less often, is storage. Every device that reports anything is producing data that has to be kept somewhere, and a great deal of it is being kept for no stated reason at all. Privacy is the word people use. Space is the question nobody asks.

steps.answer: They agree there is a risk, but describe it differently.

steps.title: Which one, or extra information?
steps.html:
Defining and non-defining — and why the comma is not decoration.

A defining relative clause tells the reader which one you mean. It is essential, and it takes no commas: A washing machine which develops a fault can report it. Remove it and you no longer know which machine.

A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about something already identified. It takes commas, and it cannot be removed without losing information — but the sentence still makes sense: Ordinary objects, which have never needed to communicate before, are now connected.

The relative pronouns: who for people, which for things, that for either — but that is only possible in defining clauses. Never Songdo, that is in South Korea…

In a defining clause, you can leave the pronoun out when it is the object: the tablet (that) you gave me. You cannot leave it out when it is the subject: the machine develops a fault is a different sentence.

Whose shows possession, for people and things alike: a car whose computer goes online. Where, when and why replace in which, on which, for which: a city where every home has broadband.

The comma changes the meaning. The engineers who design these systems disagree = only those engineers. The engineers, who design these systems, disagree = all of them, and by the way they design them.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts.

A washing machine which develops a fault can report it.
Defining: which machine. No commas.

A system that can access the GPS in your phone knows how far away you are.
Defining, with that.

Ordinary objects, which have never needed to communicate before, are connected.
Non-defining: extra information, commas.

Songdo, a city in South Korea where every home has broadband, was built to demonstrate this.
Where inside a non-defining clause.

The devices that get most attention are the silly ones.
Defining, subject pronoun — cannot be dropped.

An insulin pump, which sends readings to a doctor, is the sort of thing that will matter.
Non-defining, then defining, in one sentence.

The engineers who design these systems do not disagree.
Defining: only those engineers.

the people who worry about them
Defining, who for people.

a smoke detector which can be told to say nothing
Defining, and passive inside the clause.

a car whose in-built computer goes online
Whose works for things too.

The second worry, which is raised less often, is storage.
Non-defining.

the tablet (that) you gave me
Object pronoun — you can leave it out.

steps.title: What the comma does
steps.html:
1. Two sentences, identical except for punctuation.
  2. The engineers who design these systems do not disagree. No commas, so the clause is defining: it separates these engineers from other engineers. Only the designers are meant.
  3. The engineers, who design these systems, do not disagree. With commas, the clause is non-defining: all the engineers are meant, and the fact that they design the systems is extra.
  4. Now apply the test. Delete the clause. Sentence one becomes The engineers do not disagree — and you have lost the point, because you no longer know which engineers. Sentence two survives intact.
  5. One more check: in the non-defining version you could not write that. The engineers, that design these systems,… is wrong, always.

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least three defining relative clauses and at least two non-defining ones, punctuated correctly.
steps.html:
• Open with a device you do connect, using a defining clause.
  • Introduce the one you would not, and give the reason.
  • Use a non-defining clause to add information about a person or place.
  • Close with the comparison that settles it for you.

Useful language

  • A device which / that … can …
  • …, which is raised less often, is …
  • The people who worry about this are not …
  • Anything that can send data can …
  • a system whose … goes online when …
  • a place where every home has …
steps.modelHtml:
The one I would not connect

I have a heating system that turns itself on when my phone is within four kilometres of the flat, and I would not go back. It is the single thing in the building that has actually saved me money.

The lock is different. A door lock which can be opened from a phone is a door lock which can be opened by whoever ends up with that phone, and by anyone who can reach the system it reports to. That is not a paranoid position; it is the same sentence the engineers use.

My neighbour, who installed one last year, points out that keys get lost too. He is right, and it is still not the same. A lost key opens one door. A system that has been hacked opens every door it was ever fitted to.
